title: The Edict of Milan (313)
hook: Christianity becomes legal, and the persecuted become the favored

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantine: a sign before battle, and a church turned from hunted to favored. Your line: power changes things.

A notice goes up on a public wall in Nicomedia, a great city of the eastern empire. It's a letter from two emperors who have met at Milan and agreed on how the empire will treat religion: Constantine, who ruled the west, and Licinius, who was taking hold of the east. The writer Lactantius copied it out in full, and noted where it was posted: the same city where, by his account, an order to tear down churches and burn scriptures had been nailed up some years before. Same city, opposite message. People who had hidden their books, buried their friends and kept their heads down could walk past and read it.
screen: `A NOTICE ON A WALL IN NICOMEDIA.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the emperors grant to Christians, and to all others, the free power to follow whatever religion each person chooses. Not Christians instead of everyone else: Christians and everyone else. The reason sounds very Roman: so that whatever divine power there is in heaven may be kindly toward us and toward all who live under our rule. Then it gets practical. Meeting places and property taken from Christians are to be handed back at once, without payment, and anyone who bought one in good faith can ask the state for compensation. Freedom isn't only a sentence; it's a key returned to a door. Now the name. What we call the Edict of Milan reaches us as a letter, the copy Licinius had posted in Nicomedia. The name stuck anyway. Then the turn: the persecuted become the favored. Eusebius keeps letters from the months that follow in which Constantine sends money to clergy in Africa and frees clergy from public duties. The first letter to Timothy had asked prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life." Here was that quiet life, arriving all at once. And for good and ill: the letter's words were freedom for all. Some readers point out that later, when Christians held power, that promise didn't always hold for others. The long story has both.
screen: `AN EDICT THAT REACHES US AS A LETTER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person near you whose faith is different from yours, or who has none, and picture them on an ordinary day keeping what they keep: a prayer, a fast, a holiday, a quiet Sunday morning with no church in it. Don't argue with it; just let them be free in the picture. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, simply wish them well, as they are.
Constantine. One of the two emperors whose agreement at Milan gave Christians, and all others, freedom to follow their own religion, and handed back what had been taken.
Your line: freedom for all. Christians, and all others, in one breath. That's day seven hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Some churches pray in their services for those in authority and for people who suffer for their faith, and some Christian groups work for religious freedom for people of every faith.

chat.says: Did the Edict of Milan make Christianity the empire's official religion?
options: No. It freed Christians and all others to follow their own religion, and returned property.
Yes. From that day on, every other religion in the empire was banned by the emperors.
No. It only stopped the arrests; nothing taken from Christians was ever given back.
chat.meaning: The letter of Constantine and Licinius granted Christians and all others free choice of religion, and ordered their seized property handed back.

notes: The title carries the date 313 from the index; the spoken script states no date. Confirm the index date.

Lactantius 48: the letter of Constantine and Licinius, posted by Licinius at Nicomedia; grants Christians and all others free choice of religion 'that whatever divinity there is in heaven may be propitious', orders restoration of property without payment, with compensation for buyers. Paraphrased; confirm.
Hook says that in Nicomedia an earlier order to destroy churches and burn scriptures had been posted (Lactantius 12–13). Confirm the link and wording.

Teach says 'in later centuries, when Christians held power, that promise didn't always hold for others'. This is a general historical statement not in the cited texts; a Keeper should confirm the framing is fair, or cut it.
Trapdoor: 'not a decree issued at Milan under that title' reflects common scholarly opinion; confirm the wording.

Second editor pass: the unsourced 'in later centuries, when Christians held power' claim is now framed as what 'some readers point out'; the myth item about the name was reworded so it reads cleanly; removed the stale note about bishops traveling on imperial business, which no longer matched the script.
